name: Carlos Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a valley farm, three hundred hectares of barley and oilseed rape on the flat, and about eight hundred ewes on the slopes above the river. Mr Abara runs it, he's the tenant, and there's three of us working for him. In winter I'm mostly the shepherd, checking the flock, moving them onto turnips, sorting out lame ones. In spring and autumn I'm on the tractor for twelve hours at a time, which is where I do my thinking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like lambing, even though it nearly kills me every year. Three weeks of barely sleeping, and then you walk out one morning and the field is full of lambs jumping off the molehills. What wears me out is the paperwork for the subsidy and Mr Abara changing his mind about the cropping plan every two weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Hana, my girlfriend, she teaches at the primary school in the village. We're careful with money, we've got a good bit saved, more than a year of my wages between us. I've also got thirty ewes of my own on a paddock I rent from a neighbour, which is my little side business. I use an AI app now and then to keep track of their records, Hana showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, like the GPS on the tractor. Useful, not a miracle. I wouldn't make a fuss either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan carries on. I want to grow my own flock to a hundred ewes over the next five years, maybe rent more land, and keep working for Mr Abara while it grows. If nothing big changes, that plan still makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy another twenty ewes at the autumn sales next year and look for a second paddock to rent. Keep the savings where they are, and keep using the app for the records because it's quicker than my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use the savings for ewes or keep them separate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Separate. The ewes come out of what the flock makes, selling the lambs. The savings are for the house, one day, and Hana would kill me if I touched them for sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Mr Abara would make of it all fizzling out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be relieved, I think. He's sixty and he hates buying kit he doesn't understand. He'd say he told everyone it was a fad, even though he didn't.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, like the GPS on the tractor. Useful, not a miracle, and I wouldn't make a fuss either way.
S0.think: It means my plan carries on, growing my own flock to a hundred ewes over five years while I keep my job. If nothing big changes, that plan still makes sense.
S0.do: Buys another twenty ewes at the autumn sales and looks for a second paddock to rent. Keeps his savings separate for a future house and keeps using an AI app for flock records.
S0.quote: The savings are for the house, one day, and Hana would kill me if I touched them for sheep.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is measured and plans in five-year steps, with his own small flock as a side business. He keeps money in clear separate pots. He spoke about AI without excitement or fear, as just another tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any change, some people do well out of it and some don't, so get your head round it early. I'd probably say that to the lads at the market. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not that sort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think the tractor work goes first. There are already tractors that drive themselves on the flat, and the barley is all flat. The sheep are harder, but I reckon in a few years there'd be collars and drones doing half of what I do on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump in, but I'd watch the big farm over the river, because they always try things first. If the self-driving tractor works for them for a full season, I'd ask Mr Abara about one, and I'd want to be the one who learns it. I'd also put more into my own flock, because a man with his own sheep isn't as easy to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not too bad. It feels like something I can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a man with his own sheep isn't as easy to replace. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Abara cuts my hours, I still have the thirty ewes, and maybe more by then. It's not enough to live on, but it's something that's mine. My dad always said have one thing nobody can take off you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana think about the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be more worried about her school, honestly, because they're already trying AI tutors in some places. She'd say I'm fine because sheep don't do homework. We'd probably argue about which of us is safer.

S1.say: I'd say some people do well out of change and some don't, so get your head round it early. I'd say that to the lads at the market rather than post anything.
S1.think: The tractor work on the flat goes first, since self-driving tractors already exist. In a few years, collars and drones could be doing half of what I do on the hill.
S1.do: Watches the big farm across the river for a full season before asking his employer about a self-driving tractor, and offers to learn it himself. Puts more into his own flock as a fallback.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but it feels like something he can handle.
S1.quote: My dad always said have one thing nobody can take off you.
S1.fieldNote: His own small flock is his insurance, and he talks about it with pride. He's steady with technology: willing to learn, but only after a neighbour proves it works. He and his partner each think the other's job is safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody saw it coming this fast and we all need to keep our heads. People would be panicking at the market and I'd be the one saying, right, what can we actually do. I'd want the government to sort out some kind of income for people, because otherwise the whole place falls apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, both of us would be in trouble, Hana and me. If a robot can do lambing and teach a class of eight-year-olds, then we've both had it, just at different speeds. The savings would last us a good while, but I don't know what you save for when there's no work at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, stop buying ewes and stop renting more land, because I don't know what anything's worth any more. I'd put the money into savings and stop spending on anything big. I'd go to the machinery dealer and ask what jobs there are running the new kit, because someone has to drive the van that brings the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Still in control, just. I'd be the calm one outside and not so calm at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I can't really build anything, I can only protect what I've got. With five or ten, I'd buy land, because land doesn't go anywhere. With two, I don't even know if land's worth buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the calm one outside and not at home. What would home look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me and Hana at the kitchen table with a spreadsheet, honestly. She'd do the numbers and I'd make the tea. And we'd probably talk about moving nearer her parents, though I'd hate to leave the valley.

S2.say: I'd say nobody saw it coming this fast and we all need to keep our heads. I'd want the government to arrange some kind of income for people, or the whole place falls apart.
S2.think: Both my partner and I would be in trouble, just at different speeds. The savings would last a good while, but I don't know what you save for when there's no work at the end.
S2.do: Stops buying ewes and renting land, and moves spare money into savings while cutting big spending. Asks the machinery dealer about jobs running or delivering the new kit.
S2.feel: Anxious but just in control, calm in public and less calm at home.
S2.quote: Someone has to drive the van that brings the robots.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fast scenario he stays practical, looking for the job next to the robots rather than against them. The fast timeline stops him building and turns him to protecting what he has. He and his partner would face it together at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight, but there's time to get sorted if you start now. I'd probably say it at the young farmers' meeting, because half of them have their heads in the sand. Get skills, get some land, don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me room for one big move. I'd want to own something, a bit of land, because whoever owns the land still decides what happens on it. Even if robots do the work, they're doing it on somebody's field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look properly for a small block of land, maybe ten or fifteen hectares, and use part of the savings with a mortgage for the rest. I'd learn the new tractor systems through Mr Abara, so I'm useful while it lasts. And I'd keep the flock, maybe sell some lambs early to free up money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy, a bit worried, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Hana feel about putting the savings into land instead of a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want a house on the land, and fair enough. We'd probably look for a small place with a house, which makes it harder to find. But it would be both, a home and a bit of security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why land, when robots could farm it for anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robot still needs somewhere to work. If I own the field, I either farm it with the robot or rent it to someone who does. Either way, I'm not the one being replaced, I'm the one doing the renting.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight, but there's time to get sorted if you start now. Get skills, get some land, and don't wait.
S3.think: Five years gives me room for one big move, which is owning some land. Even if robots do the work, they're doing it on somebody's field.
S3.do: Looks in the first year for ten to fifteen hectares with a house, using part of the savings and a mortgage. Learns the new tractor systems through his employer and keeps his flock, selling some lambs early to free up money.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy and with a plan.
S3.quote: If I own the field, I either farm it with the robot or rent it to someone who does.
S3.fieldNote: His answer to AGI is ownership: land as the asset that keeps value when labour doesn't. He wants to combine it with the house he and his partner have been saving for. His centre politics show in his mix of self-reliance and his earlier call for government income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if you're sensible. That's my whole message really, be sensible, don't panic, don't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be thirty-seven, which feels fine. I'd have time to buy land slowly, build the flock, and learn the robots once they've been tested. Hana's job might change too, but she'd have time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see which machines actually work on hill sheep, then decide what to learn. Meanwhile I'd grow the flock to a hundred, save for land, and probably marry Hana, which we've been talking about anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry, but it's far enough away to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the wedding linked to all this, or just good timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. If things are going to be uncertain, I'd rather be properly tied together with Hana, for the land and the money and everything. And her gran keeps asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Of the three AGI pictures, does the extra time change what you'd do, or just how you'd feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly how I'd feel, honestly. The plan is the same, land and sheep and learning the robots. It's just that with two years I'd panic-buy it and with ten I'd do it properly.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if you're sensible. That's my whole message: be sensible, don't panic and don't ignore it.
S4.think: At thirty-seven I'd still feel fine, with time to buy land slowly, grow the flock and learn the robots once they're tested. My partner would have time to adjust as well.
S4.do: Waits a year or two to see which machines work on hill sheep before choosing what to learn. Grows his own flock to a hundred ewes, saves for land and marries his partner.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a little worry but far enough away to plan for.
S4.quote: With two years I'd panic-buy it and with ten I'd do it properly.
S4.fieldNote: He said the extra time changes how he feels more than what he'd do, which was a sharp observation. His plan stays the same across all three AGI scenarios: land, sheep and learning the robots. Marriage comes in as practical security as well as love.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd both be hit and I couldn't build anything in time. What would help is some kind of basic income while people retrain, nothing fancy. And help for young people like me to buy land before the big companies buy it all up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the sheep themselves, how they'd cope. A robot can count them, but I've seen a ewe go off her food because her lamb got sold. I don't know if a machine notices that kind of thing. Maybe it would, I honestly don't know.

headlineQuote: I've seen a ewe go off her food because her lamb got sold.
portrait: Carlos Ito, 27, is shepherd and tractor driver on a valley farm with barley, oilseed rape and eight hundred ewes, and runs a small flock of thirty ewes of his own on the side. He lives with his girlfriend Hana, a primary teacher, and they have more than a year of his wages saved. Measured and practical, he waits for neighbours to prove new kit before learning it himself. Under AGI by 2028 he turns to protecting what he has, but given five or ten years his plan is to buy land, grow his flock and marry Hana.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because both he and his partner would be hit and he couldn't build anything in time.
whatWouldHelp: A simple basic income while people retrain, and help for young people to buy land before big companies buy it all.
